questions.stem:
Consider three processes P1, P2, and P3 running identical code, as shown in the pseudocode below. A and B are two binary semaphores initialized to 1 and 0, respectively. X is a shared variable initialized to 0. Each line in the pseudocode is executed atomically.

Pseudocode of P1, P2, and P3

Assume that any of the three processes can start to execute first and context switching can happen between these processes at any arbitrary time and in any arbitrary order.

Which of the following patterns is/are possible to be generated as an outcome of the execution of these three processes?

solutionDiagram.alt: Three lock sections of A run one after another with the dollar sign printed inside the second; below them the three hash prints relayed through the gate B, with the third hash after the third star.

steps.title: What the semaphores do
steps.body: A semaphore is an integer $S$ with two operations. $\text{Wait}(S)$ lets the caller continue and lowers $S$ by 1 if $S > 0$, and otherwise makes the caller sleep until another process raises $S$. $\text{Signal}(S)$ raises $S$ by 1 and wakes a sleeper if there is one. A binary semaphore only takes the values 0 and 1. Two patterns decide this question. A semaphore that starts at 1 is a lock: the code between its Wait and its Signal runs in one process at a time. A semaphore that starts at 0 is a closed gate: every Wait on it sleeps until someone signals it. Here A (starts at 1) is the lock and B (starts at 0) is the gate.

steps.title: The stars and the dollar sign
steps.body: Everything from Wait(A) to Signal(A) is one section: print *, add 1 to X, and if X is 2 print \$ and signal B. Because A is a lock, the three sections run one after another and never mix. The first section prints * with X = 1. The second prints *, makes X = 2, and prints \$ before it releases A. The third prints * with X = 3 and prints no \$. So every possible output starts with exactly two stars and then the dollar sign, and the third star can only come after the dollar sign.

steps.title: The hashes
steps.body: The gate B stays closed until the \$ is printed, so no # appears before it. After the \$, B is 1. Each process that has left its section runs Wait(B), prints # and runs Signal(B), which passes the open gate to the next sleeper. The first two processes can print their # at any time after the \$. The third process prints its # only after its own section, so its * comes before its #. After the first three symbols the output is therefore an arrangement of one * and three # in which the * is not last: *###, #*## or ##*#. A script that tries every interleaving of the atomic lines finds exactly these three endings and no deadlock.

steps.title: Check the four options
steps.body: (A) is two stars, \$, then *###: possible. (B) is two stars, \$, then #*##: possible. (C) is two stars, \$, then ##*#: possible. (D) has three stars before the \$, but the \$ is printed inside the second section, before the third section can start: impossible. The answer is A, B and C.

shortcut.body: Spot the lock and the gate. The lock makes the \$ come right after the second $*$, so D dies at once. For the rest, the gate is open after the \$ and only the third star must precede the third hash, so every placement of the star except last works. Three options match that, which is also the key. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Believing the dollar sign can be delayed until after the third star. The \$ is printed inside the second critical section, before Signal(A), so exactly two stars precede it.

Rejecting **\$#*## because a hash seems to need all three stars first. The hash gate opens at the \$, and the first two processes have already finished their sections, so they can print $\#$ before the third star.
Rejecting **\$##*# for the same reason, or accepting only A. Two hashes can precede the third star; only the third process's own hash must wait for its star.

recognize.clues: Two binary semaphores with different starting values (1 and 0), a shared counter updated between Wait(A) and Signal(A), and a question about which output patterns are possible. The lock and the gate decide every ordering.
recognize.contrast: This is not a plain critical-section question about lost updates. The increments of X are protected by A, so nothing is lost; the open question is the order of prints, which comes from the gate B.

check.body: Trace one option by hand against the code. For **\$#*##: the first two sections print * and * with X = 2, then \$ and Signal(B); the second process then runs Wait(B), prints #, and signals B; the third section prints * with X = 3; the first and third processes then print their # in turn. Every step is allowed, so the option is possible. For ***\$###, the third section would print its star before any \$, and its increment makes X = 3, so the test X == 2 is never true again; no \$ is printed and B stays closed, which rules this option out.

questions.stem: With respect to deadlocks in an operating system, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
options: Banker’s algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks
Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed
An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource
A safe state guarantees that all processes can finish without formation of a deadlock

steps.title: Terms the statements use
steps.body: A deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for a resource that only another process in the set can release. It needs four conditions together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Prevention removes at least one of the four by a fixed rule, so deadlock cannot form. Avoidance lets all four hold but grants a request only if the system stays in a safe state, which needs each process's declared maximum in advance. In a resource allocation graph (RAG) a request edge goes from a process to a resource, and an assignment edge goes from a resource to the process that holds it. A state is safe if some order lets every process finish with the resources that are free plus those released along the way.

steps.title: Judge each statement
steps.body: (A) The Banker's algorithm checks the safe state before granting each request: that is avoidance, not prevention, so the statement is false. (B) Never letting a process hold one resource while it waits for another removes hold and wait, which is a prevention method, so the statement is true. (C) An assignment edge points from the resource to the process, so the statement is false. (D) By definition a safe state has an order in which every process finishes, so no deadlock forms if the processes follow it: true. The false statements are A and C.

shortcut.body: Check the two facts examiners twist: Banker's means avoidance, and assignment edges run resource to process. Both A and C twist them; B and D are textbook statements. Under 1 minute.

traps.text: Treating A as true because the Banker's algorithm stops deadlocks. The question separates prevention (a rule that removes a Coffman condition) from avoidance (a safety test per request), and the algorithm is avoidance.
Treating C as true by reading the edge as 'the process uses the resource'. The request edge is process to resource; the assignment edge is resource to process.
Marking D false because 'safe' sounds weaker than 'no deadlock'. A safe state guarantees that every process can finish if processes use the safe order, so no deadlock forms.

recognize.clues: The stem asks which statements about deadlocks are FALSE, and the statements name the Banker's algorithm, the hold and wait condition, an assignment edge and a safe state. Each is a definition that must be matched exactly.
recognize.contrast: Prevention and avoidance sound alike. Prevention removes one of the four conditions by a fixed rule; avoidance keeps all four possible and tests every request for safety. The Banker's algorithm belongs to the second group.

check.body: Test two statements by what the method needs as input. Prevention rules (for example, request everything at once) need no knowledge of other processes. A method that must know each process's maximum claim in advance, as the Banker's algorithm does, is working with a safety test and not with a fixed rule. For the edge direction, draw one holder: the resource box is the source of its assignment edge.

questions.stem:
Consider a system consisting of $k$ instances of a resource $R$, being shared by 5 processes. Assume that each process requires a maximum of two instances of resource $R$ and a process can request or release only one instance at a time. Further, a process can request the second instance of the resource only after acquiring the first instance.

The minimum value of $k$ for the system to be deadlock-free is ________. (answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: Two rows of five processes: with k = 5 each holds one unit and none is free, a deadlock; with k = 6 one process receives the free unit, holds two, finishes and releases both.

steps.title: When identical units deadlock
steps.body: A resource has $k$ identical instances. A process asks for one at a time, keeps what it has while it waits (hold and wait), and gives everything back only when it finishes. A deadlock is a state where every unfinished process waits for a unit and none is free, so nobody can finish and release. The rule: find the worst allocation that still leaves a deadlock, and add one unit.

steps.title: Worst case for 5 processes needing 2 each
steps.body: A process is stuck only if it holds 1 unit (it holds fewer than its maximum 2 and wants one more). The most units that can be held with every process still stuck is one each: $5 \times (2-1) = 5$. With $k = 5$ all units are held, all five processes wait for a second unit, and the system deadlocks.

steps.title: One more unit removes every deadlock
steps.body: With $k = 6$, even if each process holds 1 unit, 1 unit is free. Whoever gets it holds 2, which is its maximum, so it finishes and releases 2 units. Those 2 units let the next process finish, and so on. No allocation can leave all five stuck, because stuck processes hold at most 5 units in total. So the minimum is $k = 6$.

shortcut.body: Write $k = n(m-1) + 1$ with $n = 5$ processes and maximum claim $m = 2$: $5 \times 1 + 1 = 6$. Valid whenever all processes have the same maximum and every claim can be met by the $k$ units. 30 seconds.

traps.text: Answering 5. That is the largest number of units for which deadlock is still possible. The question asks for the smallest number that makes deadlock impossible, one more.
Answering 10, the total of all maximum claims. With 10 units nobody ever waits, which is safe but far more than the minimum.
Answering 11 or 4 by using $n \times m + 1$ or $n - 1$. Only the units a stuck process already holds, $m - 1 = 1$ each, matter.

recognize.clues: Identical units shared by several processes, each with a stated maximum claim, one unit requested at a time, and the question asks for the smallest number of units that is deadlock-free. This is the worst-case allocation argument.
recognize.contrast: The Banker's algorithm tests one given state for safety. Here no state is given, so the question is about every reachable state, which is why the worst stuck allocation plus one is the method.

check.body: Use the pigeonhole argument. If all 6 units are given out among 5 processes, some process holds at least 2, which is its maximum, so it can finish and release. With only 5 units each process can hold exactly 1, so the argument fails there. The two routes agree that 6 is the first safe value.

Each process needs at most 3 units, requests them one at a time, keeps what it holds while it waits, and may request the next unit only after it holds the previous one. questions.stem:
$P = \{P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\}$ consists of all active processes in an operating system. $R = \{R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4\}$ consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the system.

The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges.

Assignment edges: $R_1 \to P_1$, $R_2 \to P_2$, $R_3 \to P_3$, $R_4 \to P_4$ (the assignment edge $R_1 \to P_1$ means resource $R_1$ is assigned to process $P_1$, and so on for others)

Claim edges: $P_1 \to R_2$, $P_2 \to R_3$, $P_3 \to R_1$, $P_2 \to R_4$, $P_4 \to R_2$ (the claim edge $P_1 \to R_2$ means process $P_1$ is waiting for resource $R_2$, and so on for others)

Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?
options: Aborting $P_1$ makes the system deadlock free.
Aborting $P_3$ makes the system deadlock free.
Aborting $P_2$ makes the system deadlock free.
Aborting $P_1$ and $P_4$ makes the system deadlock free.

solutionDiagram.alt: Resource allocation graph with processes P1 to P4 and resources R1 to R4: solid assignment edges, dashed waiting edges, and the two cycles P1 R2 P2 R3 P3 R1 and P2 R4 P4 R2 that share P2.

steps.title: Reading a resource allocation graph
steps.body: In a resource allocation graph (RAG) a circle is a process and a square is a resource. An edge $R \to P$ means $P$ holds $R$ (assignment). An edge $P \to R$ means $P$ is waiting for $R$ (here called a claim edge). When every resource has one instance, there is a deadlock exactly when the graph has a cycle, and the processes on the cycle are the deadlocked ones. Aborting a process releases everything it holds and removes its edges, so the system is deadlock free afterwards exactly when no cycle is left.

steps.title: Find the cycles
steps.body: Follow each waiting edge to the holder of that resource. $P_1$ waits for $R_2$, held by $P_2$. $P_2$ waits for $R_3$ (held by $P_3$) and for $R_4$ (held by $P_4$). $P_3$ waits for $R_1$, held by $P_1$. $P_4$ waits for $R_2$, held by $P_2$. This gives two cycles: $P_1 \to R_2 \to P_2 \to R_3 \to P_3 \to R_1 \to P_1$ and $P_2 \to R_4 \to P_4 \to R_2 \to P_2$. Both pass through $P_2$ and $R_2$.
steps.tex: \text{cycle 1: } P_1 R_2 P_2 R_3 P_3 R_1, \qquad \text{cycle 2: } P_2 R_4 P_4 R_2

steps.title: Test each abort
steps.body: Abort $P_1$ (A): cycle 1 breaks, but $P_2$ still waits for $R_4$ held by $P_4$, and $P_4$ waits for $R_2$ held by $P_2$. Cycle 2 remains, so deadlock remains. Abort $P_3$ (B): cycle 1 breaks, cycle 2 remains. Abort $P_2$ (C): $R_2$ and $R_4$ are released and every edge of $P_2$ disappears, so both cycles are gone: $P_1$ takes $R_2$ and finishes, then $P_3$ takes $R_1$, then $P_4$ takes $R_2$. Abort $P_1$ and $P_4$ (D): $P_1$ breaks cycle 1 and $P_4$ breaks cycle 2; $P_3$ now gets $R_1$ and finishes, then $P_2$ gets $R_3$ and $R_4$. The correct statements are C and D. A script that reduces the graph after each abort gives the same result.

shortcut.body: List who waits for whom and spot the common vertex. Cycle 1 is $P_1, P_2, P_3$ and cycle 2 is $P_2, P_4$, so $P_2$ is on both. An abort that removes $P_2$, or one process from each cycle, works: C, and D (which takes $P_1$ from cycle 1 and $P_4$ from cycle 2). Aborting one process of a single cycle fails. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Aborting $P_1$ breaks the larger cycle, which is the one that looks like the deadlock. $P_2$ and $P_4$ still wait for each other through $R_2$ and $R_4$, so the system stays deadlocked.
Aborting $P_3$ has the same flaw. It also frees $R_3$ for $P_2$, but $P_2$ still needs $R_4$, which $P_4$ holds while it waits for $R_2$.
Stopping after finding one cycle. Here $P_2$ has two outstanding waits ($R_3$ and $R_4$), so there are two cycles, and every cycle must be broken.

recognize.clues: Single-instance resources, assignment edges from resource to process, claim (waiting) edges from process to resource, and a question about which aborts make the system deadlock free. Each abort is tested by whether a cycle remains.
recognize.contrast: Deadlock recovery by abort looks like deadlock avoidance, but nothing is being granted or refused here. The graph is already deadlocked and the question is which process removals cut every cycle.

check.body: Use a necessary condition for a single abort. Cycle 1 uses P1, P2 and P3, and cycle 2 uses P2 and P4. A lone abort can clear both only if the process lies on both, and the processes common to the two lists are just P2. Any single abort of P1, P3 or P4 therefore leaves one cycle. Two aborts work when one process comes from each list.

questions.stem:
Consider a multi-threaded program with two threads T1 and T2. The threads share two semaphores: s1 (initialized to 1) and s2 (initialized to 0). The threads also share a global variable x (initialized to 0). The threads execute the code shown below.

Which of the following outcomes is/are possible when threads T1 and T2 execute concurrently?
options: T1 runs first and prints 1, T2 runs next and prints 2
T2 runs first and prints 1, T1 runs next and prints 2
T1 runs first and prints 1, T2 does not print anything (deadlock)
T2 runs first and prints 1, T1 does not print anything (deadlock)

solutionDiagram.alt: Two schedules in tables: T1 takes s1 first, prints 1, blocks on wait(s2) holding s1 and T2 blocks on s1 (deadlock); T2 takes s1 first, prints 1, signals s2 and s1 and T1 then prints 2 and finishes.

steps.title: The two semaphores
steps.body: $\text{wait}(s)$ continues and lowers $s$ by 1 if $s > 0$, and otherwise blocks the caller until another thread signals. $\text{signal}(s)$ raises $s$ by 1 and wakes a blocked thread. Here $s_1$ starts at 1 and acts as a lock around the increment, the print and the end of each thread. $s_2$ starts at 0, so a $\text{wait}(s_2)$ blocks until some thread has run $\text{signal}(s_2)$. Note the trap in T1: it waits on $s_2$ while still holding $s_1$, and only T2 can signal $s_2$.

steps.title: Case 1: T1 gets s1 first
steps.body: T1 runs $\text{wait}(s_1)$, so $s_1 = 0$. It sets $x = 1$ and prints 1. Then $\text{wait}(s_2)$ finds $s_2 = 0$ and T1 blocks, still holding $s_1$. T2 starts with $\text{wait}(s_1)$, finds $s_1 = 0$ and blocks. Neither thread can move: deadlock, with exactly one line printed, 1. So option C can happen, and option A (T2 printing 2 after T1 printed 1) cannot, because T2 never gets past its first line in this case.

steps.title: Case 2: T2 gets s1 first
steps.body: T2 runs $\text{wait}(s_1)$, sets $x = 1$, prints 1, runs $\text{signal}(s_2)$ so $s_2 = 1$, then $\text{signal}(s_1)$ so $s_1 = 1$. T2 never blocks, so it always finishes. T1 then runs $\text{wait}(s_1)$, sets $x = 2$, prints 2, passes $\text{wait}(s_2)$ (which is 1) and signals $s_1$. So option B can happen. Option D (T1 stuck after T2 printed 1) cannot, because $s_2$ was signalled before T1 started. Exhaustive search over every interleaving finds exactly two outcomes: T2 prints 1 and T1 prints 2, or T1 prints 1 and both threads deadlock. The answer is B and C.

shortcut.body: Ask who takes $s_1$ first. T1 first: it blocks on $s_2$ holding $s_1$, so T2 is locked out and the system deadlocks after printing 1 (C). T2 first: it signals $s_2$ and $s_1$ without blocking, so T1 completes and prints 2 (B). A and D need the opposite of what those two cases force. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Assuming T1 can finish after printing 1. Its wait(s2) needs a signal that only T2 sends, and T2 cannot start while T1 holds s1, so T1 first always ends in deadlock.
Thinking T2 first can also deadlock T1. T2 signals s2 before it releases s1, so by the time T1 reaches wait(s2) the semaphore is already 1 and T1 passes.
Forgetting that x = x+1 and print are separate lines but sit inside the s1 lock, so no other thread can slip between them. Only the order of the lock holders matters.

recognize.clues: Two threads, a lock semaphore starting at 1 and a signalling semaphore starting at 0, and options that list printed values together with deadlock. A wait on s2 placed while s1 is still held is the feature to spot.
recognize.contrast: Do not treat this as a race on x. The increment and print sit inside the s1 lock, so the values are decided by who gets the lock first, and the danger is blocking while holding it.

check.body: Check each case with the rule that a signal must come from somewhere. wait(s2) in T1 can pass only after T2 has run signal(s2). T2 runs signal(s2) before it releases s1, so if T2 held s1 first, s2 is already 1 when T1 arrives. If T1 held s1 first, T2 cannot reach signal(s2) at all. That gives the two possible endings without listing interleavings.

T1 prints 1 and then T2 blocks forever.

variation.explanation: If T1 takes s1 first it prints 1, signals s2 and releases s1, so T2 runs to the end and prints 2. If T2 takes s1 first it blocks on wait(s2) while holding s1, and T1 blocks on wait(s1): a deadlock with nothing printed. T2 can never print before T1 because s2 only becomes 1 inside T1, and T2 cannot stay blocked after T1 has printed.

questions.stem:
Consider the following two threads T1 and T2 that update two shared variables a and b. Assume that initially a = b = 1. Though context switching between threads can happen at any time, each statement of T1 or T2 is executed atomically without interruption.

Which one of the following options lists all the possible combinations of values of a and b after both T1 and T2 finish execution?

solutionDiagram.alt: The six interleavings of T1 statements 1 and 2 with T2 statements 3 and 4, each drawn as four boxes with the values of a and b after every step; the final pairs are (4,4), (4,3) four times, and (3,3).

steps.title: What interleaving means
steps.body: Two threads share variables. Each statement runs as one indivisible step, but the scheduler may switch threads between statements. A possible run is therefore any merge of the two statement lists that keeps each thread's own order: T1's first statement stays before its second, and the same for T2. Number the statements 1: $a = a+1$, 2: $b = b+1$ (T1), and 3: $b = 2b$, 4: $a = 2a$ (T2). The rule is: try every merge that keeps 1 before 2 and 3 before 4.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The reachable pairs are exactly (4,4), (4,3) and (3,3), which is option A. The pair $(3,4)$ in options B, C and D is impossible: $a = 3$ means T1 added 1 to $a$ after T2 doubled it, so statement 4 is before statement 1; $b = 4$ means T1 added 1 to $b$ before T2 doubled it, so statement 2 is before statement 3. Together 3 < 4 < 1 < 2 < 3 is a cycle, which no merge can give. $(2,2)$ and $(2,3)$ in option D would need a thread to skip a statement.

shortcut.body: Only 6 merges, so enumerate them or reason from the two extremes: all of T1 first gives $(4,4)$, all of T2 first gives $(3,3)$, and the mixed ones give $(4,3)$. $(3,4)$ would need the order cycle 4, 1, 2, 3, 4, so it never appears. Options B, C and D each contain $(3,4)$ or an unreachable pair. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Including (3,4) because $a$ and $b$ look symmetric between the threads. The order of statements inside each thread rules it out.
Listing (3,4) instead of (3,3). A run that gives $a = 3$ doubles $b$ first, so $b$ becomes 3 and not 4.
Reading values from a step that has not finished, such as (2,2) after T1's first statement. Both threads always run to the end, so the final values are never that small.

recognize.clues: Two threads update shared variables with no lock, each statement is atomic, and the question asks for every possible final combination. That is an interleaving enumeration.
recognize.contrast: This is not a lost-update question. Each statement is a single atomic step, so no value is read stale; only the order of whole statements varies.

check.body: Run the two extremes with the numbers: T1 then T2 gives a = 2, b = 2, then b = 4, a = 4. T2 then T1 gives b = 2, a = 2, then a = 3, b = 3. Every mixed order lands between these in the sense that each variable is either added to first or doubled first. A pair where a is doubled first and b is added to first would need statements 4, 1, 2, 3 in that cyclic order, which no merge allows.

questions.stem:
Consider the two functions incr and decr shown below.

There are 5 threads each invoking incr once, and 3 threads each invoking decr once, on the same shared variable X. The initial value of X is 10.

Suppose there are two implementations of the semaphore s, as follows:

I-1: s is a binary semaphore initialized to 1.

I-2: s is a counting semaphore initialized to 2.

Let V1, V2 be the values of X at the end of execution of all the threads with implementations I-1, I-2, respectively.

Which one of the following choices corresponds to the minimum possible values of V1, V2, respectively?

solutionDiagram.alt: Timeline with a counting semaphore of value 2: D1 loads 10 and waits, five increments run in the other slot taking X to 15, D1 stores 9, then D2 and D3 store 8 and 7, so the minimum is 7.

steps.title: Semaphores and lost updates
steps.body: A semaphore $s$ is an integer. $\text{wait}(s)$ lowers it by 1, or blocks while it is 0, and $\text{signal}(s)$ raises it by 1. A binary semaphore starting at 1 lets one thread into the section at a time (mutual exclusion). A counting semaphore starting at 2 lets two threads in together. The statement $X = X + 1$ is really three machine steps: load $X$ into a register, add 1, store the result. If two threads are inside together, one can load an old value and later store over the other's newer value, so that update is lost. The rule: when more than one thread can be inside, look for the schedule that loses the updates you do not want.

steps.title: I-1: binary semaphore
steps.body: Only one thread is ever inside, so the 8 updates happen one after another and none is lost. Every order gives $10 + 5 - 3$, so the value is always 12 and $V_1 = 12$.

steps.title: I-2: counting semaphore of 2, a schedule that reaches 7
steps.body: Let a decrementing thread D1 enter, load $X = 10$ and stop. In the second slot let the five incr threads run one by one: $X$ becomes 15. D1 now stores $10 - 1 = 9$, wiping out all five increments. Then D2 loads 9 and stores 8, and D3 loads 8 and stores 7. All three decrements count and no increment does, so $X = 10 - 3 = 7$.

steps.title: Why 7 cannot be beaten
steps.body: Let $d$ be the number of decr stores finished so far. Claim: $X \ge 10 - d$ at all times. An incr store writes (the value it loaded) + 1. When it loaded, $X$ was at least $10 - d_{	ext{then}}$, and $d_{	ext{then}} \le d_{	ext{now}}$, so the stored value is above $10 - d_{	ext{now}}$ and the claim survives. A decr store writes (the value it loaded) $- 1$ and raises $d$ by 1, so the claim survives again. With 3 decrements, $X \ge 7$. Trying every interleaving of the 8 threads confirms it: with $s = 2$ the final values run from 7 to 15, and with $s = 1$ only 12 occurs. So $V_1 = 12$, $V_2 = 7$: option C.

shortcut.body: A binary semaphore means serial execution, so $V_1 = 10 + 5 - 3 = 12$ at once, which leaves C and D. For the counting semaphore, aim at the lowest value: let all increments be overwritten by one early decrement, then chain the three decrements to get $10 - 3 = 7$. About 3 minutes.

traps.text: 15 is the largest result a lost-update schedule can give, 10 + 5 with every decrement lost, so it is not a minimum. For the binary semaphore the result is 12 in every order.
Applying lost updates to I-1 as well (answer 7, 7). A binary semaphore serialises the threads, so nothing can be lost and V1 is 12.
Stopping at 8 for I-2 by letting only two decrements count. A third decrement can read 8, the value stored by the second, and store 7, so 7 is reachable.

recognize.clues: The same increment and decrement code is run under a binary semaphore and under a counting semaphore of 2, and the question asks for minimum values. The count of the semaphore decides whether lost updates are possible.
recognize.contrast: Mutual exclusion with a binary semaphore looks like the counting case but behaves differently: with one thread inside, the result is fixed, while with two inside the load-add-store steps can overlap.

check.body: Substitute a smaller case with s = 2: one incr thread and one decr thread, X = 10. Let the decr load 10 and pause, let the incr run to make X = 11, then let the decr store 9. The final value is 9, which is 10 minus the 1 decrement, and the other orders give 10 or 11. The same floor, 10 minus the number of decrements, gives 7 for 3 decrements.

questions.stem:
Consider the following threads, T1, T2, and T3 executing on a single processor, synchronized using three binary semaphore variables, S1, S2, and S3, operated upon using standard wait() and signal(). The threads can be context switched in any order and at any time.

Which initialization of the semaphores would print the sequence BCABCABCA….?

solutionDiagram.alt: Ring of three threads: T2 prints B and signals S3, T1 waits on S3, prints C and signals S2, T3 waits on S2, prints A and signals S1, which T2 waits on; only S1 starts at 1 so only T2 can start.

steps.title: A semaphore as a token
steps.body: A binary semaphore holds 0 or 1. $\text{wait}(S)$ passes only if $S = 1$ and then sets it to 0, otherwise the thread sleeps. $\text{signal}(S)$ sets it to 1 and wakes a sleeper. So a semaphore at 1 is a token that one thread can take, and a signal puts a token back. A thread can run its print only while the semaphore it waits on holds a token. The rule: to force a fixed print order, start with a token only at the thread that must print first, and let each thread pass the token to the next one.

steps.title: Who passes the token to whom
steps.body: T2 waits on S1 and signals S3. T1 waits on S3 and signals S2. T3 waits on S2 and signals S1. So the token goes T2, then T1, then T3, then back to T2. The wanted output is B (T2), C (T1), A (T3), repeated, so T2 must start: S1 = 1 and the other two 0.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: Option C has S1 = 1, S2 = 0, S3 = 0. Only T2 can pass its wait, so it prints B and signals S3. Now only T1 can run: it prints C and signals S2. Then only T3 can run: it prints A and signals S1. The cycle repeats and the output is always BCABCA.... In the other options a second thread holds a token at the start. In A (all 1) and B (S2 = 1) T3 can print A first. In D (S2 = S3 = 1) T1 or T3 can print C or A first, so the output does not have to begin with B. Trying every interleaving agrees: only C forces BCABCABCA. The answer is C.

shortcut.body: The first letter is B, printed by T2, so S1 (T2's wait) must start at 1 and no other semaphore may start at 1, because that would let a second thread print first. Only option C fits. 30 seconds.

traps.text: All three at 1 lets any thread start, so A or C could print first and the order BCA is not forced.
S1 = S2 = 1 starts T2 and T3 together, so the first letter may be A instead of B.
S2 = S3 = 1 gives the first letter to T1 or T3 (C or A), and T2 cannot start until S1 is signalled.

recognize.clues: Three infinite loops, each doing wait, print, signal on a different binary semaphore, and the question asks for the initial values that force a repeating print pattern. This is semaphores used to enforce an order.
recognize.contrast: This is not mutual exclusion on a shared section. The semaphores are passed from thread to thread as a baton, so the starting values must give the baton to exactly one thread.

check.body: Count tokens, including the one a thread is holding between its wait and its signal. Each wait moves a token out of a semaphore into the running thread and each signal puts it back, so that total stays constant. For one fixed repeating order there must be a single token, which means exactly one thread can run at the start. Options with a total of 2 or 3 let more than one thread run at the start, which breaks the order, and the single token must sit at the semaphore T2 waits on.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to deadlocks?
options: Circular wait is a necessary condition for the formation of deadlock.
In a system where each resource has more than one instance, a cycle in its wait-for graph indicates the presence of a deadlock.
If the current allocation of resources to processes leads the system to unsafe state, then deadlock will necessarily occur.
In the resource-allocation graph of a system, if every edge is an assignment edge, then the system is not in deadlock state.

solutionDiagram.alt: Resource allocation graph with two instances each of R1 and R2 and four processes: a cycle P1, R1, P3, R2 exists, yet P2 and P4 request nothing, finish, and free instances so P1 and P3 finish too, so no deadlock.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: A deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another process in the set. It needs four conditions together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. A resource allocation graph (RAG) draws a request edge from a process to a resource and an assignment edge from a resource to the process holding it. A wait-for graph draws $P \to Q$ when $P$ waits for a resource that $Q$ holds. A state is unsafe if no order lets all processes finish when each may ask for its declared maximum. The rules: a cycle proves deadlock only when every resource has a single instance, and unsafe means deadlock is possible, not certain.

steps.title: Judge each statement
steps.body: (A) True: deadlock needs all four conditions, so circular wait is necessary. (B) False: with several instances per resource a cycle is not enough. Example: two instances each of $R_1$ and $R_2$. $P_1$ holds one $R_2$ and requests $R_1$. $P_3$ holds one $R_1$ and requests $R_2$. $P_2$ holds the other $R_1$ and $P_4$ holds the other $R_2$, and both request nothing. The cycle $P_1, R_1, P_3, R_2$ exists, yet $P_2$ and $P_4$ finish and free one instance of each, so $P_1$ and $P_3$ finish as well. (C) False: unsafe says only that the worst case, every process asking for its maximum, may deadlock. A process may release resources early or never ask for its maximum, and then no deadlock occurs. (D) True: with only assignment edges nobody is waiting, so no process is blocked, and a deadlock needs blocked processes. The true statements are A and D.

shortcut.body: Keep three facts: circular wait is necessary but not sufficient; a cycle means deadlock only for single-instance resources; unsafe means possible deadlock, not certain. That kills B and C and keeps A, and D is plain because with no request edge nobody waits. 1 minute.

traps.text: Accepting B because a cycle always means deadlock. That holds only when each resource has a single instance; with several instances a process outside the cycle may release an instance and break the wait.
Accepting C by equating unsafe with deadlocked. An unsafe state may still finish if processes do not claim their full maximum, and deadlock happens only when processes actually block.
Rejecting D because many resources are held. A graph with only assignment edges has no waiting process, so it cannot contain a deadlock, however many resources are held.

recognize.clues: The stem gives no numbers, only four claims about circular wait, cycles in a wait-for graph, unsafe states and assignment-only edges. Each claim tests the exact scope of one rule.
recognize.contrast: A cycle in a resource allocation graph looks like proof of deadlock, but it is proof only with single-instance resources; an unsafe state looks like a deadlock, but it is only a risk.

check.body: Test the two surprising verdicts on tiny systems. A lone process holding 1 unit with maximum 3 and only 1 unit free is unsafe, yet if it asks for only 1 more it finishes, so unsafe does not force deadlock. A single-instance cycle P1 to R1 to P2 to R2 to P1 blocks both processes, so the cycle rule holds for one instance.

questions.stem:
Consider a computer system with multiple shared resource types, with one instance per resource type. Each instance can be owned by only one process at a time. Owning and freeing of resources are done by holding a global lock (L). The following scheme is used to own a resource instance:

Which of the following choice(s) about the above scheme is/are correct?

code.text:
function OwnResource(Resource R)
    Acquire lock L // a global lock
    if R is available then
        Acquire R
        Release lock L
    else
        if R is owned by another process P then
            Terminate P, after releasing all resources owned by P
            Acquire R
            Restart P
            Release lock L
        end if
    end if
end function

options: The scheme ensures that deadlocks will not occur.
The scheme may lead to live-lock.
The scheme may lead to starvation.
The scheme violates the mutual exclusion property.

solutionDiagram.alt: Live-lock cycle of the preempting scheme: P needs R1 then R2, Q needs R2 then R1, and each keeps terminating the other before it can finish, returning to the starting state with nobody blocked.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: Deadlock means processes wait forever for each other, so none can move. Live-lock means processes keep running and changing state but never finish. Starvation means one process is repeatedly denied what it needs. Mutual exclusion means a resource has at most one owner at a time. The scheme is a form of preemption: if someone owns the wanted resource, the requester kills the owner, takes the resource, and restarts the owner. The rule to apply: look for a place where a process waits, and then for a loop where the same events repeat.

steps.title: A: no deadlock
steps.body: A deadlock needs a process that waits while holding something. Here no process ever waits for a resource. The caller either finds R free and takes it, or kills the owner and takes it. The lock L is held for a short time and is always released. With no waiting there is no circular wait, so deadlocks cannot occur. A is correct.

steps.title: B and C: a loop of terminations
steps.body: Take two resources $R_1, R_2$. Process P needs $R_1$ then $R_2$, and Q needs $R_2$ then $R_1$. Start with P owning both resources and Q owning nothing. Q asks for $R_2$, which P owns, so Q kills P and takes $R_2$. P restarts, asks for $R_1$ (free) and gets it. P now asks for $R_2$, owned by Q, so P kills Q and takes $R_2$. P owns both resources again and Q owns nothing, which is where we started. This repeats, so each process is killed again and again, and neither completes its work although both keep running. A model of the scheme with a finish step for each process finds exactly this cycle. That is live-lock, and it is also starvation, because a process can be cut off forever. B and C are correct.

steps.title: D: mutual exclusion is kept
steps.body: At every moment each resource instance has at most one owner, because the old owner is terminated and its resources are released before the new owner acquires R. So mutual exclusion holds, and D is wrong. The correct choices are A, B and C.

shortcut.body: Scan for waiting. None exists, so no deadlock (A). A scheme that kills others to proceed can be killed back in a loop, which gives live-lock and starvation (B, C). Owners are removed before R is taken, so exclusion holds and D is out. 1 minute.

traps.text: Reading 'terminate the owner' as breaking mutual exclusion. The owner is removed first, so R still has one owner at a time.
Rejecting A because preemption sounds risky. Deadlock needs waiting, and in this scheme nobody waits.
Treating live-lock and starvation as needing a blocked process. Both can occur while every process keeps running, which is exactly what happens in the kill-and-restart loop.

recognize.clues: The code makes a requester terminate the current owner and take the resource, so no process ever waits. The choices ask about deadlock, live-lock, starvation and mutual exclusion together.
recognize.contrast: Waiting-based schemes fail by deadlock; this preempting scheme fails differently, by repeated restarts. Tell them apart by asking whether any process ever blocks.

check.body: Test the boundary cases. A single process never meets an owner, so it is never terminated and finishes; the repeating loop needs at least two processes competing for the same resource. Two processes that need disjoint resources never terminate each other either. So the trouble in B and C needs overlapping needs, as in the example. Separately, at every request the old owner is removed before the new one is set, so a resource never has two owners, which agrees with D being wrong.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pseudocode, where S is a semaphore initialized to 5 in line#2 and counter is a shared variable initialized to 0 in line#1. Assume that the increment operation in line#7 is not atomic.

If five threads execute the function parop concurrently, which of the following program behavior(s) is/are possible?
options: The value of counter is 5 after all the threads successfully complete the execution of parop.
The value of counter is 1 after all the threads successfully complete the execution of parop.
The value of counter is 0 after all the threads successfully complete the execution of parop.
There is a deadlock involving all the threads.

solutionDiagram.alt: Left: five threads each pass the first wait so S drops from 5 to 0 and all block on the second wait, a deadlock. Right: a lost update where one thread stores 1 over a count of 4, leaving counter equal to 1.

steps.title: Two things that can go wrong
steps.body: $S$ is a counting semaphore starting at 5: each wait lowers it by 1 and blocks at 0, each signal raises it by 1. Each thread does two waits, so it needs 2 units, but the pool holds only 5. Also counter++ is load, add 1, store, so two threads can overlap and one update can be lost. Two questions decide everything: can all five threads get stuck in the middle, and what values can counter end on?

steps.title: D: a deadlock is possible
steps.body: Let every thread run line 5 before any runs line 6. That is five waits and $S = 5 - 5 = 0$. Now each thread stands at line 6 holding 1 unit and needs 1 more, but nothing is free and nobody can signal. All five are blocked for ever, so D is possible.

steps.title: A: 5 is possible
steps.body: Run the threads one at a time: each does both waits, increments, signals twice. No overlap, so no lost update and $\text{counter} = 5$. A is possible.

steps.title: B: 1 is possible, C: 0 is not
steps.body: Thread a loads 0 and is paused. The other four threads then run, taking counter up to 4. Now a stores $0 + 1 = 1$, wiping out their work, and counter ends at 1. B is possible. Every store writes (a value that was read) $+ 1$, and values read are never negative, so the last store writes at least 1. Counter can never end at 0, so C is impossible. Exhaustive search of the interleavings gives counter in $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ plus the one deadlock outcome. The answer is A, B, D.

shortcut.body: Count the semaphore units: 5 threads each holding one while asking for a second drains $S$ to 0, so deadlock (D). Sequential runs give 5 (A), a lost update gives less, down to 1 (B), and every store writes at least 1, so 0 is out. 1 minute.

traps.text: Believing a lost update can erase every increment and give 0. Each store writes the loaded value plus 1, so the final value is never below 1.
Assuming 5 units are enough for 5 threads. Each thread needs 2 units at once, so when all five take one unit first, the pool is empty and every thread waits for a unit that can never come back.
Thinking the semaphore stops the lost update. S allows up to 2 threads past both waits at once (5 units, 2 per thread), so counter++ can overlap.

recognize.clues: A counting semaphore initialised to a small number, a double wait in each thread, and a non-atomic increment on a shared variable. These give both a blocking question and a lost-update question.
recognize.contrast: A binary semaphore used as a lock would keep one thread in the section and avoid both problems; here the count of 5 lets several threads in and the double wait can drain it.

check.body: Vary the thread count. With 4 threads and S = 5, four first waits leave S = 1, so one thread gets its second wait, finishes and returns units; no deadlock. With 5 threads the first waits drain S to exactly 0. So the deadlock needs all five threads, matching the stem. For counter, every store writes a loaded value plus 1, so it is at least 1 and 0 never appears.

questions.stem:
Each of a set of n processes executes the following code using two semaphores a and b initialized to 1 and 0, respectively. Assume that count is a shared variable initialized to 0 and not used in CODE SECTION P.

What does the code achieve?
options: It ensures that no process executes CODE SECTION Q before every process has finished CODE SECTION P.
It ensures that at most two processes are in CODE SECTION Q at any time.
It ensures that all processes execute CODE SECTION P mutually exclusively.
It ensures that at most n−1 processes are in CODE SECTION P at any time.

solutionDiagram.alt: Barrier with three processes: each does wait(a), count++, signal(a); the third sets count to 3 and signals b, opening the gate b; before that every process is held at wait(b), so none reaches section Q early.

steps.title: Lock and gate
steps.body: A semaphore $a$ starting at 1 is a lock: only one process at a time can be between $\text{wait}(a)$ and $\text{signal}(a)$. A semaphore $b$ starting at 0 is a closed gate: $\text{wait}(b)$ blocks until someone does $\text{signal}(b)$. The code is a barrier: a place where every process must arrive before any may go on. The rule: find the one event that opens the gate, and ask who can do it.

steps.title: Counting arrivals
steps.body: Each process finishes section P and then runs $\text{wait}(a)$, adds 1 to $\text{count}$, and signals $a$. The lock makes the additions safe. Only the process that makes $\text{count} = n$ runs $\text{signal}(b)$, and this happens only after all $n$ processes have added 1, that is, after all $n$ finished P.

steps.title: Passing the gate
steps.body: Before the $n$-th arrival, $b = 0$, so every process that gets to $\text{wait}(b)$ waits there. Once $b = 1$, a process passes, then runs $\text{signal}(b)$ at once, which puts the token back for the next one. So the processes pass one after another, and none reaches Q before all have finished P. A is true.

steps.title: The other options
steps.body: B is false: after the gate opens, $b$ is restored by every process, so all $n$ may be in Q together, not only two. C is false: P sits before $\text{wait}(a)$, with no lock, so any number may be in P together. D is false for the same reason: all $n$ can be inside P at once. The answer is A.

shortcut.body: Spot the pattern: a counter under a lock, then the last arrival signals a gate that each process re-signals. That is a one-use barrier, and a barrier means nobody enters Q until all have left P. 30 seconds.

traps.text: Thinking the signal(b) after wait(b) limits Q to two. It does the opposite: it keeps the gate open for everyone.
Confusing the lock a with a lock on P. The lock covers only the count update, and section P is outside it.
Thinking the gate holds back the last process. The last arrival is the one that opens it, and nothing limits how many are inside P before that.

recognize.clues: Semaphore b starts at 0, a shared count is raised under the lock a, only the process that makes count equal n signals b, and every process re-signals b after passing. That is a gate opened by the last arrival.
recognize.contrast: It resembles mutual exclusion because of the lock a, but a only protects the counter; the gate b decides who enters section Q.

check.body: Run n = 2. First process: wait(a), count = 1, no signal, signal(a), then wait(b) blocks since b = 0. Second process: count = 2, signal(b) makes b = 1, signal(a), wait(b) passes with b = 0, signal(b) makes b = 1, enters Q. The first process now passes wait(b) too. Nobody entered Q before both had finished P.

questions.stem:
Consider three concurrent processes P1, P2 and P3 as shown below, which access a shared variable D that has been initialized to 100.

The processes are executed on a uniprocessor system running a time-shared operating system. If the minimum and maximum possible values of D after the three processes have completed execution are X and Y respectively, then the value of Y – X is _____________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two schedules from D = 100: P2 loads 100, P1 and P3 run to reach 130, then P2 stores 50 giving the minimum; and P1 stores 120, P3 loads 120, P2 stores 50, P3 stores 130 giving the maximum.

steps.title: Why the answer is not one number
steps.body: A time-shared system can switch between processes at any machine instruction. The statement $D = D + 20$ is three instructions: load $D$ into a register, add 20, store the register into $D$. If a switch happens between the load and the store, another process may change $D$ in the meantime, and the store then overwrites that change. This is a lost update. The rule: the final value is whatever the last store wrote, so we choose which stores to lose.

steps.title: Minimum X
steps.body: Let P2 load 100 first and wait. Run P1 and P3 completely, which takes $D$ to 130. Then P2 stores $100 - 50 = 50$, overwriting both. Only the decrement counted, so $D = 100 - 50 = 50$. It cannot go lower: P2 can only load a value of at least 100, and P1 and P3 only add. So $X = 50$.

steps.title: Maximum Y
steps.body: Now lose P2's update and keep both increments. P2 loads 100 and waits. P1 runs: $D = 120$. P3 loads 120 and waits. P2 stores 50. P3 stores $120 + 10 = 130$. The value 130 is the top: every store adds at most 20 or 10 to a value that was already at most 130 (induction), and P2 only lowers. So $Y = 130$. The reachable final values, found by trying every interleaving, are 50, 60, 70, 80, 110, 120 and 130.

shortcut.body: Best case for the largest value: the decrement is lost, $100 + 20 + 10 = 130$. Best case for the smallest: both increments are lost, $100 - 50 = 50$. The difference is $80$. 30 seconds.

traps.text: Taking the sequential result 80 as both X and Y and answering 0. Without synchronisation, the interleavings give different results.
Reporting Y alone (130) or X alone (50). The question asks for the difference $Y - X$, which is 80.

recognize.clues: Three unsynchronised processes update one shared variable on a time-shared uniprocessor, and the question asks for the minimum and maximum possible results. That is a race condition and lost updates.
recognize.contrast: With a lock around each statement the result would be the single value from serial execution; without it the interleavings give a range, so tell them apart by checking for mutual exclusion.

check.body: Bound the range by the serial result. Any serial order gives $100 + 20 - 50 + 10 = 80$, which lies between the two extremes. The top is reached by keeping every increase and dropping the decrease, the bottom by keeping only the decrease. So the gap is the sum of the sizes of all three changes: $20 + 10 + 50 = 80$.

questions.stem: Consider the following snapshot of a system running n concurrent processes. Process i is holding Xi instances of a resource R, 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Assume that all instances of R are currently in use. Further, for all i, process i can place a request for at most Yi additional instances of R while holding the Xi instances it already has. Of the n processes, there are exactly two processes p and q such that Yp = Yq = 0. Which one of the following conditions guarantees that no other process apart from p and q can complete execution?
options: Xp + Xq < Min {Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}
Xp + Xq < Max {Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}
Min (Xp, Xq) ≥ Min {Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}
Min (Xp, Xq) ≤ Max {Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}

solutionDiagram.alt: Number line of freed instances: p and q release Xp plus Xq, and another process can finish only if its extra request Yk is at most that sum; the condition puts every Yk to the right of the sum.

steps.title: What can finish
steps.body: A process can finish only if it can obtain all the extra instances it may still ask for, $Y_k$, at the same time. All instances are in use, so nothing is free now. Processes $p$ and $q$ need nothing more ($Y = 0$), so they finish and give back $X_p + X_q$ instances. That is all the free supply there is, until some other process finishes. The rule: a process $k$ can finish only if $Y_k \le$ the free supply.

steps.title: Turn the rule round
steps.body: No other process may finish. The first one to finish would need $Y_k \le X_p + X_q$. To stop every one of them we need $Y_k > X_p + X_q$ for all other $k$. The smallest $Y_k$ is the easiest to satisfy, so it is enough to check the minimum: $X_p + X_q < \min Y_k$. Then all $Y_k$ are above the supply and nobody else can finish.

steps.title: Check against the options
steps.body: A is exactly this condition. B uses the maximum: it only says the sum is below the largest $Y_k$, but a process with a small $Y_k$ could still finish. C and D compare $\min(X_p, X_q)$ with other values, but the supply is the sum $X_p + X_q$, so they do not decide who can finish. The answer is A.

shortcut.body: The freed supply is $X_p + X_q$. To block everyone, even the process with the smallest extra need must be blocked, so compare against the minimum: option A. Anything with a Max or a $\min(X_p, X_q)$ is wrong. 30 seconds.

traps.text: Using the Max. That blocks only the process with the largest request, and one with a small request could still finish.
Comparing min(Xp, Xq) with a minimum Y. The supply is the sum of both, not the smaller one, and the inequality points the wrong way for a guarantee.
Comparing min(Xp, Xq) with the maximum Y. This does not use the sum, and says nothing that stops a small request from being met.

recognize.clues: All instances are in use, two processes need nothing more, and the question asks which condition stops every other process from completing. This is the safe-sequence test with symbolic numbers.
recognize.contrast: It looks like a pure resource counting problem, but unlike the minimum-resources question it compares needs against the freed supply, not against the total.

check.body: Test with numbers. Let $X_p = 2$ and $X_q = 1$, so the supply is 3. With other requests 4 and 5 nobody else can run, and the condition holds since $3 < 4$. Change one request to 3: that process now fits in the supply and finishes, and the condition fails since $3 < 3$ is false. The boundary agrees with the condition.

questions.stem: Consider a system with 3 processes that share 4 instances of the same resource type. Each process can request a maximum of $K$ instances. Resource instances can be requested and released only one at a time. The largest value of $K$ that will always avoid deadlock is ____.

solutionDiagram.alt: Four unit slots for three processes: with K = 2 each holds one and one unit stays free so a process can reach its maximum and finish; with K = 3 the holding 2, 1, 1 uses all four units and every process still wants one more.

steps.title: What a deadlock needs here
steps.body: A resource type has 4 identical instances. A process asks for them one at a time, keeps what it already holds while it waits, and gives everything back only when it has reached its maximum $K$ and finished. A deadlock is a state in which every unfinished process is waiting for an instance and no instance is free, so nobody can finish and release. The rule: a process holding $K$ instances can always finish, so deadlock needs every process to be stuck holding at most $K-1$ while all instances are taken. Deadlock is therefore possible exactly when $n(K-1) \ge R$ for $n$ processes and $R$ instances, and it is impossible when $n(K-1) < R$, that is $n(K-1)+1 \le R$.

steps.title: Set up the numbers
steps.body: Here $n = 3$ processes and $R = 4$ instances. Deadlock is avoided for every possible order of requests when the three processes together cannot use up all four instances while all of them are still short of $K$. The most they can hold while every one of them is still unfinished is $3(K-1)$ instances.

steps.title: Solve and check the boundary
steps.body: The inequality gives $K - 1 \le 1$, so $K \le 2$. Check $K = 2$: every process holds at most 1, so at most 3 of the 4 instances are held and 1 is always free. Whoever receives it reaches its maximum 2, finishes and returns 2 instances, and the others follow. No deadlock. Check $K = 3$: the holding $(2, 1, 1)$ uses all 4 instances, each process holds fewer than 3, each wants one more, and none is free. That is a deadlock. Larger $K$ leaves even more room for it. The largest safe value is 2.

shortcut.body: Use $n(K-1)+1 \le R$: $3(K-1)+1 \le 4$ gives $K \le 2$. 20 seconds. It is safe only when every process has the same maximum $K$, there is one resource type, and each process asks one instance at a time, as here.

traps.text: Answering 3. For $K = 3$ the allocation $(2, 1, 1)$ already deadlocks. 3 is the smallest $K$ for which deadlock can happen, not the largest for which it cannot.

Answering 1 from $\lfloor 4/3 \rfloor$. That divides the instances evenly, which would only be needed if every process had to hold its full maximum at the same time. Processes finish one after another and release, so 2 still works.
Answering 4 because the total of 4 instances covers one process's maximum. A single process is never the problem. Deadlock comes from the three processes each holding part of what they need.

recognize.clues: Identical processes with the same maximum K, one resource type with a fixed count, and requests made one instance at a time. The question asks for the largest K that always avoids deadlock.
recognize.contrast: The Banker's algorithm tests one given state for safety; here no state is given, so we need the worst case over all states instead.

check.body: Use a second route, pigeonhole. If all 4 instances are allocated among 3 processes, some process holds at least 2. With maximum 2 that process holds its full need, so it can finish and release. With maximum 3, holding 2 is still short of 3, so that argument fails. The two routes agree on where safety ends.

questions.stem:
In a system, there are three types of resources: E, F and G. Four processes P0, P1, P2 and P3 execute concurrently. At the outset, the processes have declared their maximum resource requirements using a matrix named Max as given below. For example, Max[P2,F] is the maximum number of instances of F that P2 would require. The number of instances of the resources allocated to the various processes at any given state is given by a matrix named Allocation.

Consider a state of the system with the Allocation matrix as shown below, and in which 3 instances of E and 3 instances of F are the only resources available.

From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which one of the following is true?
options: The system is in safe state.
The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of E were available
The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of F were available
The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of G were available

solutionDiagram.alt: Four boxes in a chain: P0, P2, P1 and P3 each run in turn because their need fits the available vector, and the available vector grows from (3,3,0) to (4,3,1), (5,3,4), (6,4,6) and (8,4,6).

steps.title: What a safe state is
steps.body: Each process has declared a maximum (Max) for every resource type. Allocation is what it holds now. Need is what it may still ask for, $\text{Need} = \text{Max} - \text{Allocation}$. Available is the number of free instances of each type, written as a vector $(E, F, G)$. A process can run to the end if its Need is at most Available in every type. When it ends it returns its whole Allocation, so Available grows. A state is safe if some order of the processes lets every one of them finish this way; deadlock avoidance only grants requests that keep the state safe. The test: repeatedly pick any process whose Need fits in Available, finish it, add its Allocation back, and see whether all four get picked.

steps.title: Compute Need and Available
steps.body: Subtract Allocation from Max row by row: P0 $(4,3,1)-(1,0,1) = (3,3,0)$, P1 $(2,1,4)-(1,1,2) = (1,0,2)$, P2 $(1,3,3)-(1,0,3) = (0,3,0)$, P3 $(5,4,1)-(2,0,0) = (3,4,1)$. The stem says only 3 instances of E and 3 of F are available, so no G is free: Available is $(3,3,0)$.

steps.title: Find a finishing order
steps.body: Only P0 and P2 fit now: P1 needs 2 of G and P3 needs 4 of F. Run P0: need $(3,3,0) \le (3,3,0)$, then Available $= (3,3,0)+(1,0,1) = (4,3,1)$. Run P2: need $(0,3,0) \le (4,3,1)$, Available becomes $(4,3,1)+(1,0,3) = (5,3,4)$. Run P1: need $(1,0,2) \le (5,3,4)$, Available becomes $(5,3,4)+(1,1,2) = (6,4,6)$. Run P3: need $(3,4,1) \le (6,4,6)$, Available becomes $(8,4,6)$. All four finished, so the order P0, P2, P1, P3 is a safe sequence.

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body: The state is safe, so option A is true. Options B, C and D all begin with 'the system is not in safe state', which is false, so each is false whatever follows. The answer is A.

shortcut.body: Write Need = Max - Allocation, then run a process whose Need fits, add its Allocation back and repeat. A safe order appears after one pass: P0, P2, P1, P3. A safe state makes B, C and D false at once. About 2 minutes. Always compare Need, not Max, with Available.

traps.text: Comparing Max with Available instead of Need. P0's Max in E is 4 against 3 available, which looks like one E is missing. P0's Need in E is only 3.
Testing every process against the starting Available only. P3 needs 4 of F against 3 free, which looks like one F is missing. P3 runs last, after P0, P2 and P1 have returned their F.
The same single-shot test on P1, which needs 2 of G while G is 0. P1 runs after P0 and P2 release G, so no extra G is needed.

recognize.clues: Allocation and Max matrices for four processes and three resource types, plus an Available vector, and the question asks about safety from the viewpoint of deadlock avoidance.
recognize.contrast: Deadlock detection looks at processes already waiting; avoidance asks whether some order could still finish everyone, using Need rather than current requests.

check.body: Test a different order. Start from Available $(3,3,0)$. Run P0 (Need $(3,3,0)$ fits), giving $(4,3,1)$. Run P1 (Need $(1,0,2)$ fits), giving $(5,4,3)$. Run P3 (Need $(3,4,1)$ fits), giving $(7,4,3)$. Run P2 (Need $(0,3,0)$ fits), giving $(8,4,6)$. A second safe sequence exists, and it ends at the total the system owns.

questions.stem:
Consider the following solution to the producer-consumer synchronization problem. The shared buffer size is $N$. Three semaphores empty, full and mutex are defined with respective initial values of 0, $N$ and 1. Semaphore empty denotes the number of available slots in the buffer, for the consumer to read from. Semaphore full denotes the number of available slots in the buffer, for the producer to write to. The placeholder variables, denoted by P, Q, R, and S, in the code below can be assigned either empty or full. The valid semaphore operations are: wait() and signal().

Which one of the following assignments to P, Q, R and S will yield the correct solution?
options: P: full, Q: full, R: empty, S: empty
P: empty, Q: empty, R: full, S: full
P: full, Q: empty, R: empty, S: full
P: empty, Q: full, R: full, S: empty

solutionDiagram.alt: Producer and consumer boxes with a buffer between them: the producer waits on full (free slots, starts N) and signals empty (items, starts 0), the consumer waits on empty and signals full, shown as two arrows in opposite directions.

steps.title: Counting semaphores as slot counters
steps.body: A semaphore is an integer. $\text{wait}(S)$ lowers it by 1 when it is above 0 and otherwise puts the caller to sleep. $\text{signal}(S)$ raises it by 1 and wakes a sleeper. In a bounded buffer of $N$ slots two counters do the work: one counts the free slots and one counts the filled slots. The producer must wait for a free slot and, after adding, announce one more filled slot. The consumer must wait for a filled slot and, after taking, announce one more free slot. The mutex only keeps the two from touching the buffer at the same instant. Read the names from the stem, not from habit: here empty counts the slots the consumer can read from, that is the items, and starts at 0; full counts the slots the producer can write to, that is the free slots, and starts at $N$. The names are the reverse of the usual textbook ones.

steps.title: Fill in the placeholders
steps.body: The producer waits for a free slot, so P = full. After adding it announces an item, so Q = empty. The consumer waits for an item, so R = empty. After taking it frees a slot, so S = full. That is option C.

steps.title: Check it behaves
steps.body: At the start empty is 0, so a consumer that arrives first sleeps at wait(empty) and cannot read from an empty buffer. The producer can run $N$ times, each time lowering full and raising empty, and the $(N+1)$-th wait(full) sleeps because the buffer is full. Each consumed item raises full and wakes the producer. A script that tries every interleaving for $N = 2$ and all 16 assignments of the four placeholders finds that only P = full, Q = empty, R = empty, S = full gives neither a deadlock nor an overflow or underflow of the buffer.

steps.title: Why the other three fail
steps.body: A: the producer waits on full and signals full, so it never sleeps and overfills the buffer, while the consumer waits on empty that nobody raises and sleeps forever. B: the producer waits on empty, which starts at 0, and sleeps forever, while the consumer waits on full, which starts at $N$, and reads from an empty buffer. D: the roles are swapped, the consumer waits on the free-slot counter and reads from an empty buffer at once. Only C is correct.

shortcut.body: The producer needs a free slot, and the free-slot counter is the one that starts at $N$: full. So P = full, which leaves A or C. A has the producer wait on full and signal full, the same semaphore, so it can never block: out. C remains. 1 minute. Take the meaning from the stem's definitions, since the names are the reverse of the textbook.

traps.text: Choosing a pair where the producer waits and signals the same semaphore. The producer never blocks, so the buffer overflows, and the consumer waits on a counter nobody raises.

Choosing a pair where each side waits and signals the same semaphore, the same lure as A. The producer waits on empty, which starts at 0, so it sleeps at once, and the consumer waits on full, which starts at $N$, so it reads from an empty buffer.

Using the classic textbook naming, where empty counts free slots: the producer waits on empty and signals full, the consumer waits on full and signals empty. That is P = empty, Q = full, R = full, S = empty. Here empty starts at 0 and means items, so the producer sleeps at once and the consumer reads from an empty buffer.

recognize.clues: Two semaphores with opposite initial values (0 and N) plus a mutex, a bounded shared buffer, and placeholders to fill so that producer and consumer neither overfill nor underflow it.
recognize.contrast: The textbook version names the free-slot counter empty. Here the stem reverses the names, so the mapping must come from the stem definitions and the initial values, not from the usual labels.

check.body: Swap test: take P = empty and Q = full. empty starts at 0, so the producer blocks at its very first wait and never adds anything; the buffer stays empty and the system makes no progress. The chosen assignment avoids this. Invariant test: with P = full, Q = empty, R = empty, S = full, empty + full equals N at every moment outside a wait/signal pair. It starts at 0 + N, a producer step lowers full by 1 and raises empty by 1, and a consumer step lowers empty by 1 and raises full by 1. Both counters stay at 0 or above, so items never exceed N and never go below 0.

questions.stem:
A system shares 9 tape drives. The current allocation and maximum requirement of tape drives for three processes are shown below:

Which of the following best describes current state of the system?
options: Safe, Deadlocked
Safe, Not Deadlocked
Not Safe, Deadlocked
Not Safe, Not Deadlocked

solutionDiagram.alt: Four rows of nine tape-drive cells: at first two are free, then P3 finishes and five are free, then P1 finishes and eight are free, then P2 finishes and all nine are free.

steps.title: Safe, unsafe and deadlocked
steps.body: Each process has a maximum number of drives it may ask for (Maximum Requirement) and holds some now (Current Allocation). Need is what it may still ask for, $\text{Need} = \text{Maximum} - \text{Allocation}$. A state is safe if some order exists in which every process can get its whole Need from the free drives plus the drives returned by processes that finished earlier in the order. A state is unsafe if no such order exists. A deadlock is different: processes are already waiting on one another and can never continue. A safe state can never be deadlocked, because the finishing order is a way out. An unsafe state is only at risk of deadlock, and is not necessarily deadlocked.

steps.title: Free drives and Need
steps.body: Allocated: $3 + 1 + 3 = 7$ of the 9 drives, so 2 are free. Need: P1 $7-3 = 4$, P2 $6-1 = 5$, P3 $5-3 = 2$.

steps.title: Look for a finishing order
steps.body: With 2 free, only P3 can be served (need 2). P3 finishes and returns 3, so 5 are free. Now P1 (need 4) fits; it finishes and returns 3, so 8 are free. P2 (need 5) fits and finishes, so all 9 are free. The order P3, P1, P2 lets every process finish: the state is safe.

steps.title: Deadlocked or not
steps.body: A safe state is never deadlocked, and no process is waiting on another right now. So the state is safe and not deadlocked: option B.

shortcut.body: Free = 9 - 7 = 2. The smallest Need is 2 (P3), so P3 can finish and free 5, which covers the other Needs 4 and 5. Safe. Safe means not deadlocked. B, in about a minute. It is safe to stop after the first step because the 5 freed drives cover both remaining Needs, 4 and 5.

traps.text: Safe and deadlocked cannot both hold. A safe state has a finishing order, which is exactly the way out of a deadlock.
Seeing 2 free drives against Needs of 4 and 5 and concluding that everyone is stuck. P3 needs only 2, finishes, and its drives unblock the rest.
The same mistake of judging by the 2 free drives alone, then correctly noting that nobody is waiting yet. The state is safe, so 'not safe' is wrong.

recognize.clues: One resource type with a single count of 9, a table of current allocation against maximum requirement, and a question about whether the present state is safe.
recognize.contrast: This is the safety test, not deadlock detection on a resource allocation graph. Detection uses current requests; the safety test uses the maximum claims to see whether some finishing order exists.

check.body: Try the order P1, P2, P3 instead. With 2 free drives P1 needs 4 and cannot start, so a wrong first pick gets stuck, which is why the order matters. Now try a second safe order from the start: P3, P2, P1. P3 runs with 2 free and returns 3, so 5 are free; P2 needs 5 and fits, and returns 1, so 6 are free; P1 needs 4 and fits, and returns 3, so all 9 are free. A second order that also ends with the whole pool agrees with the first.

questions.stem: A multithreaded program P executes with $x$ number of threads and uses $y$ number of locks for ensuring mutual exclusion while operating on shared memory locations. All locks in the program are non-reentrant, i.e., if a thread holds a lock $l$, then it cannot re-acquire lock $l$ without releasing it. If a thread is unable to acquire a lock, it blocks until the lock becomes available. The minimum value of $x$ and the minimum value of $y$ together for which execution of P can result in a deadlock are:

solutionDiagram.alt: One thread T and one lock l: T locks l, then runs lock(l) a second time, blocks, and waits for l, which only T could release, so it waits forever.

steps.title: Locks, blocking and deadlock
steps.body: A lock gives mutual exclusion: while a thread holds it, no other thread can hold it. $\text{lock}(l)$ takes the lock if it is free and otherwise blocks the caller until the lock is released. $\text{unlock}(l)$ releases it. A non-reentrant lock does not recognise its own holder, so a thread that already holds $l$ and calls $\text{lock}(l)$ again blocks like any other caller. A deadlock is a state in which some threads are blocked forever, each waiting for something that only a blocked thread can do. The rule for the question: find the smallest program that reaches such a state, and compare its $x$ and $y$ with the options.

steps.title: The smallest possible program
steps.body: A program that uses locks for mutual exclusion has at least 1 thread and 1 lock, so $x \ge 1$ and $y \ge 1$. Can $x = 1$, $y = 1$ deadlock? Yes. Let the single thread T run lock(l) twice. The first call takes the lock. The second call finds l held and blocks. The holder is T itself, and T is now blocked, so the unlock that would free l is never reached. T waits for a release that only T can make: a deadlock with one thread and one lock.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: The minima are reached together at $(x, y) = (1, 1)$, which is option D. A script that tries every lock and unlock program of up to four operations finds the deadlock at $(1,1)$ at once. The familiar two-thread, two-lock cycle (one thread holds $l_1$ and wants $l_2$, the other holds $l_2$ and wants $l_1$) is a deadlock too, but it is not the smallest.

shortcut.body: Ask for the smallest numbers first: 1 thread and 1 lock. Then ask whether those can deadlock; with a non-reentrant lock, locking twice does it. D, in 30 seconds. The shortcut fails if the locks were reentrant: then (1,1) could not deadlock and the classic (2,2) cycle would be the answer.

traps.text: Believing a deadlock needs two locks held in opposite order. With a non-reentrant lock, one lock taken twice already blocks the holder.
Believing it needs two threads, one holding the lock and one waiting. The holder eventually releases it, so the waiter proceeds; there is no deadlock unless the holder itself blocks on l.
Recalling the textbook cycle of two threads and two locks. It is a sufficient pattern but not the minimum, because the non-reentrant rule makes 1 and 1 enough.

recognize.clues: Words such as non-reentrant, blocks until the lock becomes available, and minimum x and minimum y. Together they ask for the smallest configuration that can wait forever.
recognize.contrast: The classic two-thread, two-lock cycle is circular wait between different threads. Here the wait is on a lock the same thread holds, so the cycle has length one and needs no second thread.

check.body: Compare with a reentrant lock. If the same one-thread, one-lock program ran on a reentrant lock, the second lock(l) would succeed, unlock(l) would run twice, and the program would finish. Only the non-reentrant rule changes the outcome, so that rule is what causes the deadlock. In the wait-for graph (an arrow from a thread to the thread that holds what it wants) T points at the holder of l, which is T: a self-loop, a cycle of length one.

variation.stem: A multithreaded program has $x$ threads and $y$ locks used for mutual exclusion. All locks are reentrant: a thread that holds a lock may acquire it again, and must release it as many times as it acquired it. A thread that cannot get a lock blocks until it is free, and every thread releases all locks it takes. Which values of $x$ and $y$ are the smallest for which execution can result in a deadlock?

A script that tries every balanced lock and unlock program found a deadlock only at $x = 2, y = 2$.
